title: CCNP Cybersecurity core (350-201 CBRCOR v1.2) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from Cisco's public 350-201 CBRCOR v1.2 exam topics (dated Jul 2, 2025; https://learningcontent.cisco.com/documents/marketing/exam-topics/350-201-CBRCOR-v1.2_02July2025.pdf, checked 2026-11-27). Not real exam questions. Cisco doesn't publish the number of items on the real exam; this is a 100-item stand-in in 120 minutes with 4 hands-on items (log review, terminal, ordering and diagram). Practice only in your own lab or on legal ranges such as TryHackMe, never on work networks.

q.q: A phishing playbook says: "Start: a user reports a message to the abuse mailbox. Owner: Tier 2 analyst. Done when: the message is removed from all mailboxes and the case is documented." Which part of the playbook is the user report?
o: The escalation path, the route to more senior staff
An escalation path says who gets the case when the first team can't solve it. Nothing in the text describes one.
The trigger, the event that starts the play
Right. A trigger tells the team when to begin. Here, the report from the user starts the work.
The exit criteria, the conditions that show the play is finished
Exit criteria are the "done when" part: removal from all mailboxes and a documented case.
The owner, the role responsible for the steps
The owner is the Tier 2 analyst. A report from a user is an event, not a role.

q.q: A playbook step reads: "If the sender domain was registered fewer than 30 days ago AND the link's reputation is Untrusted, quarantine every copy of the message. Otherwise, close as benign." What kind of step is this?
o: A decision point that sends the play down one of two branches
Right. The condition picks between quarantine and close. Real playbooks use branches like this so analysts don't make the call from memory.
A trigger that starts the play when a new domain appears
The play has already started. This step runs inside it.
A fixed action that runs the same way for every message
A fixed action has no "if". This step has a test and two outcomes.
A metric that measures how long phishing cases stay open
A metric counts or times something. This step acts on a message.

q.q: A SOC manager asks how a playbook differs from a runbook. Which answer is most accurate?
o: They are the same document, and the name depends on whether the team uses a SIEM or a SOAR
The names are not tied to a tool. The scope of each document is what differs.
A playbook covers only technical commands, and a runbook covers only management approvals
A playbook includes both people and technical actions. Neither document is limited to one side.
A playbook guides the response to a scenario. A runbook gives exact steps for one task.
Right. The playbook decides who acts and when. The runbook, such as "isolate a host in the EDR console", is a task inside it.
A playbook is used before an incident and a runbook is used only after the incident closes
Both are used during response. The runbook is not an after-action report.

q.q: A play for a suspected compromised laptop includes the step "cut the host off from the network but keep it powered on, then list its running processes." Which tool category does this step need?
o: A NetFlow collector that records conversations between hosts
NetFlow shows who talked to whom. It can't cut off the host or read its process list.
A web application firewall in front of the company website
A WAF filters web requests going to servers. It has no control over a laptop's network or processes.
A vulnerability scanner that runs on a weekly schedule
A scanner finds missing patches and bad settings. It does not isolate a host or list live processes.
Endpoint detection and response (EDR), such as Cisco Secure Endpoint
Right. EDR can isolate a host while keeping a management channel open, and it shows live process data.

q.q: A play step says: "Find out whether 203.0.113.9 has appeared in any proxy or DNS log across the unit in the past 30 days." Which tool does the analyst need?
o: A password vault, to look up the stored credentials
A vault stores secrets. It has no network history.
The SIEM, to search the collected logs
Right. A SIEM holds normalized logs from many sources, so one search covers the proxy and DNS data.
A patch manager, to list devices missing updates
A patch manager reports update status. It does not hold network log history.
A malware sandbox, to run the address in an isolated machine
A sandbox runs files and shows what they do. It can't search past proxy or DNS logs.

q.q: An analyst receives an unknown Word file attached to a report and must learn what it does when opened, without risk to the network. Which tool does the playbook call for?
o: An email gateway that quarantines the message
A gateway can block or hold mail, but it doesn't show what a file does when opened.
A threat intelligence feed that lists known bad domains
A feed helps with known indicators. It can't show what a new file does.
A sandbox such as Cisco Secure Malware Analytics
Right. A sandbox runs the file in an isolated system and records its file, registry and network actions.
A firewall rule that blocks the sender's address
A block may stop the next message, but it tells the analyst nothing about the file.

q.q: At 02:10, the SIEM raises: user "tsmith" was added to Domain Admins by service account svc-deploy. No change ticket exists. What should the privilege-escalation playbook have the analyst do first?
o: Mark the alert as a false positive because service accounts are trusted
A service account making an unapproved admin change is a warning sign, not a reason to close.
Reset every Domain Admin password in the company before looking at anything else
A broad reset is disruptive and doesn't remove the unapproved membership that already exists.
Run a full antivirus scan on the domain controller and wait for the result
A scan doesn't undo an account change, and waiting leaves the new admin active.
Remove the group membership, disable svc-deploy, and save the event logs
Right. This stops the abuse of admin rights while keeping the evidence of who did what.

q.q: A hospital's public web portal is hit by a flood of UDP traffic that fills the unit's 1 Gbps Internet link. The web servers have low CPU use. Which playbook action helps most?
o: Ask the ISP or a scrubbing service to filter the flood upstream
Right. The link is full before packets reach the servers, so the filtering must happen upstream of the link.
Reboot the web servers to clear their connection tables
The servers aren't the bottleneck, and a reboot only makes the portal unavailable.
Raise the TCP backlog setting on the web servers
A TCP setting helps with SYN floods. This flood is UDP and the link is the choke point.
Block the attacking sources one by one in the web server's host firewall
Packets must cross the full link before the host firewall sees them, so this does not relieve the link.

q.q: A town's public website homepage was replaced with a protest message. The playbook says to restore from a known-good backup. What must happen BEFORE the restore?
o: Copy the altered files and the web server logs to protected storage
Right. The altered files and logs show what changed and how the attacker got in. A restore would overwrite them.
Post a statement on the unit's social media explaining the cause
The cause isn't known yet, and communications follow the plan after facts are confirmed.
Re-image the web server from the golden image and review it later
Re-imaging first destroys the evidence, and the same flaw may be reused.
Edit the homepage by hand to remove the message and keep the rest
A manual edit hides the problem and ignores other changes the attacker may have made.

q.q: A cloud provider wants to sell its software service to U.S. federal agencies. Which program sets a standard security assessment and authorization process for such cloud services?
o: GDPR
GDPR covers personal data of people in the EU. It doesn't set a U.S. federal cloud authorization process.
PCI DSS
PCI DSS applies to organizations that handle cardholder data.
FISMA
FISMA covers agency information systems as a whole. FedRAMP is the standard authorization program specifically for cloud services.
FedRAMP
Right. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program is the U.S. government program for cloud service authorization.

q.q: A U.S. company with no office in Europe runs an online store that ships to customers in France and Germany and keeps their names and addresses. Which regulation most likely applies to how it handles that data?
o: SOX, because the company takes online payments
SOX is about financial reporting at public companies. Taking payments does not bring it into play.
FISMA, because the company stores data on servers
FISMA applies to federal agencies and their contractors, not to a private online store.
GDPR, because it covers personal data of people in the EU
Right. GDPR reaches companies outside the EU that offer goods to people there.
HIPAA, because the data includes names and home addresses
HIPAA covers health information held by certain health organizations. Names and addresses alone don't trigger it.

q.q: Which TWO costs are typically covered under the first-party part of a cyber risk insurance policy? (Choose two.)
o: Buying better security tools after the incident so it doesn't happen again
Upgrades beyond the pre-loss condition are called betterment and are commonly excluded.
Losses tied to controls the company said it had but didn't have
Gaps between the application answers and reality are a common reason for denied claims.
Replacing servers that wore out from normal age
Normal wear and aging are maintenance costs, not cyber losses.
Forensic investigation and incident response services after a breach
Right. Insurers usually pay for outside responders who find out what happened.
Notifying affected customers and offering credit monitoring
Right. Notification and monitoring costs after a data breach are standard coverage items.

q.q: A unit's renewal form asks whether MFA protects all remote access. The answer was "yes," but after a ransomware claim the insurer finds a VPN with no MFA. What is the most likely result?
o: The premium is unchanged and the insurer simply asks for MFA next year
A misstatement about a control is a claim problem, not just an item for next year.
The insurer may deny or reduce the claim because the application was inaccurate
Right. Insurers underwrite on the answers given. A wrong answer about a required control can void coverage.
The insurer pays only for the hardware that was damaged
Cyber policies cover response, recovery and liability costs more than hardware.
The insurer pays in full because ransomware is always covered
Coverage depends on the policy terms and the truth of the application.

q.q: Which situation has the HIGHEST risk?
o: A patched public web server that hosts only a lunch menu for the base cafeteria
There is exposure but little value and no known weakness.
A server with patient records that is fully patched and sits behind a well-configured firewall
The asset is valuable, but with no weakness the chance of loss is low.
A patient-records server with an unpatched flaw that attackers are exploiting
Right. High asset value, a real weakness, and an active threat combine into the highest risk.
An unpatched test server that holds no real data and has no network connection at all
The weakness is real, but there is no threat path and nothing valuable to lose.

q.q: A file server is worth $200,000. A flood would destroy 25% of its value. Flooding is expected once every five years. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
o: Right. Single loss expectancy is $200,000 x 0.25 = $50,000. Multiply by a yearly rate of 0.2 to get $10,000.
This adds the asset value and the single loss instead of multiplying the factors.
This is the single loss expectancy, the loss from one flood, not the yearly figure.
This multiplies asset value by the yearly rate and skips the 25% damage factor.

q.q: After a risk analysis, a unit buys a cyber insurance policy to cover the remaining financial loss from a possible breach. Which risk treatment is this?
o: Mitigation
Mitigation lowers likelihood or impact with controls, such as patching. Insurance does neither.
Avoidance
Avoidance means stopping the activity that creates the risk.
Acceptance
Acceptance means leaving the risk in place without action. Buying a policy is an action.
Transfer
Right. Insurance moves part of the financial impact to another party. The risk itself still exists.

q.q: Analysts have confirmed ransomware on three file servers. According to the incident response workflow, what comes next?
o: Preparation, by writing the response plan
Preparation happens before incidents. The plan should already exist.
Containment, to stop the spread while evidence is kept
Right. After detection and analysis confirms the incident, the team limits the damage before cleanup.
Lessons learned, by holding a review meeting
The review comes at the end, after the incident is resolved.
Recovery, by restoring the file servers from backup
Restoring before the threat is contained and removed risks losing the restored data again.

q.q: During an incident, which action belongs in eradication, not containment?
o: Blocking the command-and-control domain at the DNS server
Blocking a domain limits the attacker's access and is a containment step.
Removing the malware and closing the vulnerability that let it in
Right. Eradication removes the cause so it can't return.
Moving an infected host to a quarantine VLAN
Quarantine stops the spread. It does not remove the infection.
Capturing a memory image of the infected host
Evidence collection supports analysis and is done early, before changes.

q.q: An analyst copies the disk of a compromised server for the investigation. Which item best keeps the image trustworthy as evidence?
o: A screenshot of the analyst's desktop during the copy
A screenshot doesn't prove the image's content stayed unchanged afterward.
A note stating that the analyst holds a security certification
A certification may support credibility, but it doesn't document the handling of this item.
A hash taken at copy time and a chain-of-custody log of who handled it
Right. The hash shows the image was not changed, and the log shows who held it and when.
The incident ticket number written on the storage device
A ticket number helps with tracking but doesn't prove integrity or custody.

q.q: A SOC detects phishing alerts within minutes but needs about nine hours to contain them, mostly waiting for manager approval to disable accounts. Which metric shows the problem, and which change fits?
o: Mean time to respond; pre-approve routine containment steps
Right. The delay is between detection and action. Pre-approved steps remove the wait for routine cases.
Mean time to detect; add more sensors and log sources to find alerts faster
Detection is already fast, so more sensors would not fix the delay.
False positive rate; tune the detection rules to produce fewer low-value alerts
Alerts are valid. The delay comes after they are confirmed.
Mean time between failures; replace the aging servers
This is an equipment reliability measure and has no link to the approval delay.

q.q: An attacker first gained access on March 3. The SOC got an alert on March 17, isolated the host on March 18, and finished restoring systems on March 21. What is the time to detect for this incident?
o: 15 days
This runs from the start to containment, which mixes detection with response.
1 day
This is the time from detection to containment, a response measure.
18 days
This runs from the start to full recovery, so it is the whole incident length.
14 days
Right. Time to detect runs from the start of the intrusion to the alert: March 3 to March 17.

q.q: Several federal agencies with a shared mission use one cloud environment, run by one of the agencies, that only they may use. Which cloud type is this?
o: Private cloud for a single organization
A private cloud is used by one organization. Here several agencies share it.
Public cloud
A public cloud is offered to the general public or many unrelated customers.
Community cloud
Right. A community cloud serves a group with shared requirements and is limited to that group.
Hybrid cloud
A hybrid cloud combines two or more different cloud types. The scenario is one shared environment.

q.q: A unit keeps case records in its own on-site cloud and uses a public cloud for short bursts of processing. A VPN links the two. Which description fits?
o: Community cloud
A community cloud is shared by a group of organizations with common needs.
Hybrid cloud
Right. It combines a private cloud and a public cloud that are linked.
Multi-tenant public cloud only
Part of the environment is on-site and private, so it isn't only a public cloud.
Private cloud only
The public cloud part means it isn't only private.

q.q: A SOC will monitor a virtual machine rented as IaaS and a managed database rented as PaaS. Which statement is correct?
o: On IaaS the customer handles the guest OS. On PaaS the provider does.
Right. IaaS leaves the guest OS to the customer. PaaS moves it to the provider.
The provider patches the guest OS on both, so the SOC only watches user logins
On IaaS the customer owns the guest OS, so the provider doesn't patch it.
Neither needs monitoring, since cloud services secure themselves
The customer always remains responsible for data, access and configuration.
The customer patches the OS on both, because the provider only supplies power
On PaaS the provider runs and patches the platform underneath.

q.q: A SOC wants to detect someone creating a new access key in the unit's cloud account. Which log source shows this?
o: The hypervisor's own host log, kept by the provider
Customers don't get the provider's hypervisor logs.
Flow logs that record network connections between subnets
Flow logs describe traffic, not account configuration changes.
Syslog from the guest operating system of a virtual machine
Guest logs show activity inside the VM, not management actions on the account.
The cloud control-plane audit log that records API and console actions
Right. It records who called which management action, including new keys.

q.q: The SOC cannot install its endpoint agent on a managed (PaaS) database service. What is the usual reason, and what should the SOC use instead?
o: The provider runs the host, so the SOC relies on the service's own logs
Right. PaaS hides the host, so the customer watches the service's audit logs, access settings and alerts.
Cloud services block all logging, so the SOC watches only the network edge
PaaS services offer activity logs. Watching only the edge would miss them.
The agent is not licensed for databases, so the SOC buys a database-specific agent
Licensing isn't the issue. The customer has no access to the host at all.
The database is too small to run an agent, so the SOC uses larger hardware
The limit is about who controls the host, not about size.

q.q: A software-as-a-service company wants an independent auditor's report on its security and availability controls that customers can request during their own reviews. Which report fits?
o: A SOC 2 report
Right. SOC 2 reports describe an independent auditor's view of a service provider's controls.
A FedRAMP authorization
FedRAMP is for federal use, and the company's goal here is a report for any customer.
A SOX certification
SOX is about financial reporting at public companies, not service security and availability.
A PCI DSS attestation
PCI DSS applies to organizations that handle cardholder data.

q.q: A ransomware attack stops a unit's billing system for four days. Which cyber insurance coverage pays for the income lost during that time?
o: Notification cost coverage
This pays for letters and credit monitoring, not for lost income.
Betterment coverage
Betterment coverage pays for upgrades that remove the flaw after a breach. It doesn't pay for income lost while systems are down.
Business interruption coverage
Right. It pays for lost income and extra costs while systems are down.
Third-party liability coverage
This covers claims against the company, not its own lost income.

q.q: A SOC wants to show leaders each month whether its response is improving. Which set of measures fits best?
o: The number of alerts closed and the number of analysts on shift
Closing more alerts doesn't show whether threats were found or handled faster.
Mean time to detect and mean time to respond, tracked month over month
Right. Time to detect and time to respond show speed, and the trend shows change.
Total log volume collected and the storage space it uses
Volume measures the size of the system, not the quality of the response.
The count of SIEM rules and their average age
Rule counts say little about how quickly incidents are found and handled.

q.q: Which statement describes a private cloud?
o: Cloud services that unrelated customers share over the Internet
That describes a public cloud.
Cloud infrastructure shared by organizations with a common mission
That describes a community cloud.
Two or more different cloud types that are linked together
That describes a hybrid cloud.
Cloud infrastructure that a single organization uses, hosted on site or by a provider
Right. A private cloud serves one organization, wherever it is hosted.

q.q: A unit holds tabletop exercises and builds a contact list so that it is ready before any incident happens. Which phase of the incident response workflow is this?
o: Detection and analysis
This phase begins when something suspicious is noticed.
Containment
Containment limits the damage of an incident that is already under way.
Preparation
Right. Plans, training and contact lists are built before an incident.
Lessons learned
This phase reviews an incident after it has been handled.

q.q: A unit moves a web application from its own servers to a PaaS platform. Which task still belongs to the unit?
o: Patching the host operating system under the platform
On PaaS the provider patches the host operating system.
Managing who can use the application and protecting its data
Right. Access and data stay with the customer in every cloud model.
Maintaining the physical datacenter and its power
The provider runs the datacenter in every cloud model.
Updating the runtime that the platform provides
On PaaS the provider updates the runtime.

q.q: A SOC wants to group 40,000 endpoints by how they behave, with no labeled examples, so unusual machines stand out. Which technique fits?
o: Signature matching against a list of known file hashes
Signatures find known items. They can't find machines that merely behave unusually.
Supervised classification trained on malware labels
Supervised models need labeled examples, which this team doesn't have.
Linear regression that predicts next month's alert count
Regression predicts a number. It doesn't group machines by behavior.
Unsupervised clustering of endpoints by their process and network features
Right. Clustering finds groups in unlabeled data, and machines far from every group are outliers.

q.q: A phishing-detection model flags 1% of incoming mail. Analysts find that 95% of the flagged mail is harmless. Which measure is low?
o: Latency
Latency is how long a decision takes. It says nothing about how many flags are correct.
Precision
Right. Precision is the share of flagged items that are truly bad. Here only 5% are, so precision is low.
Recall
Recall is the share of all bad mail that the model catches. The scenario doesn't say how much it missed.
Throughput
Throughput is how much mail the model processes per second.

q.q: A team wants to spot unusual spikes in hourly DNS query volume, given a normal pattern that changes between weekdays and weekends. Which approach fits?
o: A fixed threshold of 10,000 queries for every hour of the week
A single limit would miss weekend spikes that are small but unusual and would fire on busy weekday peaks.
Reverse DNS lookups for each address that was queried in the log
These identify names for addresses. They don't measure unusual volume.
Time-series anomaly detection using a weekly baseline
Right. It compares each hour with what is normal for that hour and day.
A decision tree trained on web page categories and file types
Page categories don't describe query volume over time.

q.q: New virtual machines are built from an image made eight months ago, and each needs about 40 patches on first boot. What is the best fix?
o: Turn off automatic updates in the image so the machines match
Matching old, unpatched machines doesn't make them safer.
Patch every new machine by hand after it has been deployed
This leaves each machine exposed until the patches finish and adds manual work every time.
Clone a production server and use it as the next image
A running server carries its own data, accounts and drift, which would be copied into every new machine.
Rebuild the golden image on a schedule and keep versions
Right. A regularly rebuilt, versioned image starts new machines in a known, current state.

q.q: Which TWO belong in a hardened machine image? (Choose two.)
o: Unused services disabled and default accounts removed or renamed
Right. Fewer services and no default logins mean fewer ways in.
Sample data and test accounts so testers can log in right away
Test accounts and sample data carry into production if they stay in the image.
Packet-capture and compiler tools to speed up troubleshooting
Extra tools help an intruder as well, so they stay out of a standard image.
A shared local administrator password in the build notes for emergencies
A shared password that many people know can't be tied to one person and is easy to leak.
The finished image stored in a controlled repository, with a recorded hash
Right. Access control and a hash let teams confirm that the deployed image is the approved one.

q.q: Which evidence best shows whether a server's configuration has drifted from its approved baseline?
o: A port scan report that was run on this server about a year ago
An old scan is out of date and shows open ports, not full configuration settings.
A configuration compliance scan comparing it with the baseline
Right. The scan checks each setting against the approved standard and lists differences.
The server's purchase order, warranty record and asset tag number
These show when it was bought, not how it is set up now.
The date of the server's last antivirus scan and its result
A scan date shows malware checks ran, not whether settings changed.

q.q: A posture check on a laptop finds disk encryption off and the EDR agent stopped five days ago. The OS is fully patched. What should the access policy do?
o: Allow normal access, because the OS is fully patched and up to date
Patches alone don't make up for missing encryption and a stopped agent.
Block all of the user's accounts across every company system
The device is the problem, not the user's identity. Restricting the device is enough.
Limit its network access until encryption and the agent work again
Right. A device that fails required controls shouldn't reach normal resources until fixed.
Wipe the laptop right away and issue the user a replacement
A wipe is out of proportion and may destroy useful evidence if the agent stopped for a bad reason.

q.q: An authorized penetration test showed a tester moving from a user VLAN to the database server over SMB. Existing controls were a perimeter firewall and EDR. What gap does this reveal?
o: No filtering between the user and server networks
Right. Traffic between internal zones wasn't restricted, so one foothold reached sensitive servers.
No perimeter firewall at the Internet edge of the network
A perimeter firewall already exists, and the movement happened inside.
No password policy for the accounts on the database server
Passwords aren't mentioned, and the finding is about the open network path.
Missing disk encryption on the laptops used by staff
Encryption protects stored data. It would not block network movement.

q.q: A red team using Kerberoasting (offline cracking of service account tickets) raised no alert. What is the best improvement?
o: Add detection for bursts of service ticket requests using RC4
Right. Event 4769 logs service ticket requests, so a spike or weak encryption type can be flagged.
Block all Kerberos traffic between clients and domain controllers
Kerberos is how the domain works, so blocking it would stop normal logons.
Disable the red team's account and rerun the same test next week
That hides the gap and doesn't help the SOC detect real attackers.
Increase the log retention on the web proxy to cover a full year
Proxy logs don't contain the Kerberos requests.

q.q: A Department of Defense system must follow a mandated hardening baseline for its operating system. Which resource does the unit use?
o: A CIS Benchmark
CIS Benchmarks are consensus guides that many groups use, but they aren't the DoD mandate.
The applicable DISA STIG
Right. Security Technical Implementation Guides are the DoD's required configuration standards.
NIST SP 800-61
SP 800-61 is a guide for handling incidents, not for hardening.
MITRE ATT&CK
ATT&CK describes attacker behavior and is not a configuration baseline.

q.q: A security engineer needs a catalog of security and privacy controls from which to select safeguards for a new system. Which NIST publication is the right one?
o: SP 800-88 covers how to sanitize media before reuse or disposal.
SP 800-30 explains how to carry out risk assessments.
SP 800-61 is about computer security incident handling.
Right. SP 800-53 is the catalog of security and privacy controls for systems and organizations.

q.q: A vendor has released a patch for a flaw that attackers are exploiting on Internet-facing VPN gateways. The next scheduled maintenance window is a month away. What is the best recommendation?
o: Wait for the monthly window so the change process isn't disturbed
A month of exposure to active attacks is too long for a front-door device.
Patch all gateways at once without testing, then watch for problems
Skipping testing on a critical access path can cause an outage for all remote staff.
Patch early after a quick test, using vendor mitigations until then
Right. Active exploitation of an exposed device justifies an emergency window with limited, fast testing.
Skip the patch because the gateways are behind a firewall
VPN gateways must be reachable from the Internet, so the firewall doesn't protect them from this flaw.

q.q: A control system runs an operating system the vendor no longer supports, and no patch exists for a serious flaw. Which recommendation is best?
o: Isolate it and block the exploit with IPS rules
Right. Compensating controls reduce exposure when patching isn't possible.
Install a patch designed for a different Windows version
A patch for another version may fail or damage the system.
Reboot the system every night to clear out any infection
A reboot doesn't remove an infection or stop a new exploit.
Accept the risk and leave the system as it is, since it runs fine
A serious flaw with no fix calls for protective steps, not silence.

q.q: A web server needs only HTTPS and administrator SSH, but a scan shows ports 22, 23, 443 and 445 open, and the clock service running. Which TWO services should be disabled? (Choose two.)
o: The time synchronization client
Accurate time keeps logs and certificates reliable, so it stays on.
HTTPS on port 443 for the site
HTTPS is the server's purpose.
Telnet on port 23
Right. Telnet sends passwords in clear text, and SSH already provides remote administration.
SSH on port 22
SSH is the secure admin channel the server needs.
SMB file sharing on port 445
Right. A web server has no need to share files, and SMB has a long history of attacks.

q.q: A domain controller has no printing role. Which service should be disabled to reduce its attack surface?
o: Kerberos Key Distribution Center
The KDC issues tickets for domain logons, so a domain controller needs it.
Windows Time
Time service keeps Kerberos working, so it stays on.
DNS Server, when the domain relies on it
Active Directory depends on DNS, and removing it would break name resolution.
Print Spooler
Right. Microsoft advises turning it off on domain controllers that don't print, because it has had serious flaws.

q.q: After an incident, the review shows the attacker moved from one user workstation to many others over SMB. Which change best limits this?
o: Add a second Internet connection for failover and extra bandwidth
A second link improves availability and does nothing about internal movement.
Deny workstation-to-workstation traffic with host firewalls
Right. Workstations rarely need to talk to each other, so denying it removes the attacker's path.
Raise the minimum password length requirement for all user accounts
Longer passwords don't stop movement that uses stolen tokens or a vulnerable service.
Schedule the antivirus scans to run each evening
The scan time doesn't affect network paths between hosts.

q.q: A unit wants to shrink the part of its network that a payment-card audit covers. Which design helps most?
o: Install antivirus on every server and workstation across the entire company
Antivirus is useful but doesn't reduce which systems are in scope.
Rename the card systems on the main network so auditors don't notice them
Hiding systems doesn't change their risk, and misleading an audit is a serious violation.
Put the card-data systems in their own segment behind firewall rules
Right. Segmentation keeps the audit scope to the segment and what connects to it.
Move the card systems onto the guest Wi-Fi network
Guest networks are less trusted, so this increases risk.

q.q: A server was infected through a phishing email on another machine, and now it calls out to random Internet hosts. Which network control would most reliably block that traffic, including callbacks to hosts that no feed has listed yet?
o: A longer DHCP lease time for the whole server subnet
Lease length affects address assignment, not outbound filtering.
A DNS sinkhole for domains already known to be malicious
A sinkhole helps with listed domains, but traffic to a bare IP address or a new domain still gets out.
Default-deny egress rules with a destination allowlist
Right. Servers talk to a short list of places, so denying all other outbound traffic cuts off the callbacks.
IPS signatures for known command-and-control families
Signatures catch only known families, and a new callback destination would pass.

q.q: A visitor plugs a personal laptop into a wall jack in a meeting room and receives an address on the internal network. Which control prevents this?
o: WPA3 on the wireless network
WPA3 protects Wi-Fi, but the visitor used a wired jack.
IEEE 802.1X port authentication through network access control
Right. The switch port stays closed until the device proves who it is.
DNS filtering of known bad categories
It limits where users can go after connecting. It doesn't stop the connection.
A signature update for the intrusion prevention system
An IPS looks at traffic content and doesn't decide which devices may connect.

q.q: A pipeline scanner finds a cloud access key in a commit that was pushed to a shared repository three days ago. What is the best response?
o: Revoke and replace the key, then add secret scanning
Right. Anyone who has read the repository could have copied the key, so it must be treated as exposed.
Delete the file from the repository in a new commit
The key stays in the repository history and remains usable.
Make the repository private and keep using the same key
People and tools with earlier access may already have the key.
Tell the team not to use the key and wait for it to expire
A key with no expiry is still valid, and asking people not to use it doesn't stop an attacker.

q.q: A build step flags that the application bundles an old third-party library with a known vulnerability. Which kind of test found this?
o: Dynamic application security testing (DAST) of the running site
DAST sends requests to a running app to find issues. It doesn't inventory libraries.
Static application security testing (SAST) of the unit's own source code
SAST analyzes code the team wrote, though it may not examine bundled libraries for published flaws.
A penetration test of the production network
A pen test is a manual, scheduled exercise and isn't a build step.
Software composition analysis (SCA)
Right. SCA lists the open-source components in an application and compares them with known vulnerabilities.

q.q: Which pair do threat intelligence platforms commonly use to share indicators with partners?
o: STIX to describe the data, TAXII to carry it
Right. STIX is the structured language and TAXII is the transport for exchanging it.
OVAL to describe the data, SCAP to carry it
These are used for vulnerability and configuration checks.
TAXII to describe the data, STIX to carry it
This reverses the roles of the two standards.
SNMP to describe the data, syslog to carry it
These are for device management and logging, not threat intelligence exchange.

q.q: A TIP receives 50,000 new IP indicators a day from several feeds. Pushing all of them to the firewall blocked a legitimate content delivery network. What is the best fix?
o: Push every indicator and let analysts reverse the false blocks when users complain
This turns users into the detection method for false positives.
Send the indicators to the firewall only on weekends
Timing doesn't improve the quality of the indicators.
Score and age indicators, filter by confidence and relevance, then push only the vetted set
Right. Scoring and expiry keep stale or low-confidence indicators from blocking real services.
Stop using threat intelligence feeds completely
Feeds are valuable when managed, so removing them gives up detection.

q.q: An analyst uses an approved internal AI assistant to turn a 40-page threat report into a list of indicators. What should happen before any of them are blocked?
o: Remove all private IP addresses from the list, then block everything that remains
Removing private addresses is a good check but doesn't verify the remaining items.
Check each indicator against the source report and a trusted lookup
Right. AI output can contain errors or invented items, so it must be checked before enforcement.
Ask the assistant the same question again and use the matches
Repeating a question can repeat the same error.
Push them to the firewall because the model has seen millions of reports
Training volume doesn't prevent mistakes in a given answer.

q.q: A model gives every DNS name a risk score. Which feature most strongly suggests a domain generated by an algorithm?
o: A name hosted by a major provider with a valid certificate
Valid certificates and major hosting are common for legitimate sites, though not proof.
A name registered several years ago with stable records
Age and stable records point toward a legitimate domain.
A name that matches the company brand with a common top-level domain
That describes a normal or lookalike domain, not a random string.
A long random-looking name with many failed lookups
Right. Algorithmic domains tend to be random strings, and most of them don't exist, so lookups fail.

q.q: A cloud storage container with scanned contracts was left publicly readable for weeks. Logs show no sign that anyone downloaded files. Which term fits best?
o: Data exfiltration, because an attacker took the data
Exfiltration means a deliberate transfer out by an attacker, and there is no sign of one.
Data in use, because the files were opened
Data in use means data being processed in memory by an application or user.
Data remanence, because deleted files were left behind
Remanence is leftover data after deletion. Nothing was deleted.
Data leakage, because the data was exposed to unauthorized parties
Right. Leakage is unintended exposure, and it counts even if copying can't be shown.

q.q: An analyst has a spreadsheet of case numbers open and copies cells into a chat window. Which state is the data in?
o: At rest
At rest means stored on disk or in a database and not being accessed.
In archive
Archived data is long-term storage, which is a kind of data at rest.
In use
Right. Data open in an application and being handled by a user is in use.
In motion
In motion means moving over a network, such as during a file upload.

q.q: A unit wants to stop staff from copying files labeled "Controlled" to personal USB drives. Which DLP type enforces this?
o: A web application firewall
A WAF protects web applications from attacks and isn't a data loss tool.
Host (endpoint) DLP
Right. An agent on the device can see and block copies to removable media.
Email-only DLP in the mail gateway
This inspects messages. It has no view of local file copies.
Network DLP at the Internet edge
Network DLP sees traffic crossing the network, and USB copies never touch it.

q.q: A network DLP appliance can't read an employee's HTTPS upload of a customer list to a personal webmail site. What allows it to inspect the content?
o: TLS inspection at the proxy so uploads can be scanned
Right. Decrypting at an approved inspection point lets DLP rules examine the content.
Turning up the logging level on the DLP appliance and proxy
More logging records metadata but can't reveal encrypted content.
Blocking all outbound traffic on TCP port 443 for every user
That would stop the web for everyone, including normal business use.
Hashing every file on the file server each night
Hashes help identify known files but don't let the appliance read an encrypted upload.

q.q: An IDS rule for port scans fires 2,000 times a day because the unit's approved vulnerability scanner at 10.4.4.20 triggers it. What is the best tuning step?
o: Exempt the scanner address and document the exception
Right. A documented, narrow exception removes known noise and keeps the rule for everyone else.
Raise the rule's severity so analysts review it first
More attention on known noise worsens alert fatigue.
Delete the scanner's logs every night
The alert still fires. Removing logs also hurts auditing.
Disable the port scan rule on every IDS sensor in the unit
A global disable removes detection of real scanning.

q.q: A mail filter lets through phishing sent from domains registered a few days ago. Which policy change helps most?
o: Scan the attachments of every message with antivirus only
Phishing pages are often reached by a link with no attachment, so an attachment scan would miss them.
Allow mail from any sender with a valid SPF record
Attackers can set up valid SPF records on their own domains.
Quarantine mail from domains younger than 30 days
Right. New domains are cheap for attackers to create, so domain age is a useful risk signal.
Add a banner to every external message saying it came from outside
A banner helps users, but it doesn't stop mail from new domains from being delivered.

q.q: Firewall, proxy and EDR logs name the source address as src_ip, SourceAddress and ip.src. Which process maps all three to one field so one search finds them?
o: Retention for 12 months
Retention is how long data is kept.
Enrichment with geolocation data
Enrichment adds extra context, such as a country, to existing values.
Compression of old log files
Compression saves storage space and does nothing for field names.
Normalization to a common schema
Right. Normalization gives equal data the same field name, so correlation and searches work across sources.

q.q: A regulation requires one year of logs. Analysts mostly search the last 90 days. Which storage design meets both needs with sensible cost?
o: Keep all logs on the fastest search storage for as long as possible
This meets the rule but at a high cost, and it keeps data longer than needed.
Keep 90 days searchable and archive the rest at lower cost
Right. A tiered design gives fast search for recent data and low-cost retention for the full year.
Delete logs after 90 days to save space on the SIEM
That breaks the one-year requirement.
Keep logs on each device and collect them only when someone asks
Devices overwrite logs, and an attacker can erase them, so collecting only on request is not reliable.

q.q: The SIEM has shown no alerts from the firewall for six days. Later, the team learns the firewall stopped forwarding logs after an upgrade. Which SIEM control would have caught this sooner?
o: A longer retention period for firewall logs
Keeping data longer doesn't help when no data arrives.
A dashboard that displays the number of blocked connections
A count of blocked events can't show that no events arrive.
An alert when a log source sends no events for a set time
Right. A silence alert tells the team a source is no longer reporting.
A rule that deletes duplicate events
Removing duplicates doesn't detect missing data.

q.q: Which log source in the SIEM is most valuable for spotting lateral movement by remote desktop between servers?
o: Windows logon events (4624, type 10) from the target hosts
Right. Event 4624 with type 10 records a remote interactive logon, showing who logged in from which source.
The web server's access log for the unit's public site
It records web requests and doesn't record logons to the operating system.
The DNS server's query log for external names looked up by staff
It shows name lookups, not who logged in to a server.
The badge reader log for the server room door
It shows physical entry and has nothing about network logons.

q.q: A Tier 1 analyst confirms that an EDR alert shows credential dumping from memory on a domain controller. What should the workflow require next?
o: Email the domain controller's owner and wait for an answer
The owner should be informed, but the SOC's own escalation path comes first.
Escalate to Tier 2 or the incident lead with the evidence
Right. A confirmed high-impact finding on a key system needs senior responders at once.
Wait until the end of the shift to batch it with other alerts
Delay gives the attacker time to use the stolen credentials.
Close the alert after adding a note about the finding to the ticket
Closing a confirmed serious detection leaves the attacker active.

q.q: In an automated phishing playbook, which action should require a human to approve it first?
o: Checking the sender's domain age and URL reputation
Lookups carry little risk and are a standard automated step.
Adding the message and ticket details to the case record
Case notes are routine record keeping and need no approval.
Extracting the URLs and file hashes from the message
This is a safe read-only step suited to automation.
Disabling the account of a senior officer who clicked the link
Right. This action can disrupt critical work and affect someone with broad authority, so a person decides.

q.q: A commanding officer wants a one-page security dashboard for a monthly meeting. Which panel best fits that audience?
o: A list of the alert rule names that fired the most this month
Rule names are meaningful to the SOC but not to a non-technical leader.
Trend of open critical incidents and time to contain them
Right. Leaders need risk and performance in plain terms, with a target to compare against.
The packet count per hour for each switch in the building
This is network engineering detail, not a security outcome.
A live table of raw firewall events with source and destination ports
Raw events are for analysts and hide the overall picture.

q.q: An executive dashboard shows "blocked events: 4.2 million this month" rising each month and is presented as proof of improved security. Why is this misleading?
o: It counts activity, not risk reduction, and says nothing about incidents or exposure
Right. A larger count may mean more noise, and it doesn't show what mattered or how fast the team responded.
Leaders should see only a red, yellow or green status with no figures
A simple status can help, but the problem here is that this figure doesn't measure risk.
Blocked events are always errors that should be zero
Blocks are expected, since the controls are working as designed.
Blocked events are counted only when an attack succeeds, so the figure is wrong
Blocked events are counted whenever a control stops something, so the figure is right. The issue is what it can't show.

q.q: What is the core method behind user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA)?
o: Require a second factor for every login to every application
MFA is an authentication control, not an analytic method.
Block a fixed list of Internet addresses at the firewall
A blocklist is a static control and doesn't learn behavior.
Compare activity with a baseline from the user's own history and peers
Right. Deviations from normal behavior for that user or role raise a risk score.
Match every file the user opens against a database of known malware hashes
That is signature matching, which is a different technique.

q.q: A service account that always logs on from one application server, without interactive sessions, now logs on interactively at a workstation. Which UEBA finding fits?
o: Normal behavior, since any account may log on anywhere
Service accounts aren't expected to behave like people.
Privilege escalation, because the account gained a higher role
Nothing in the event shows a change of role or group. What changed is how and where the account logs on.
Anomalous account behavior: new logon type from a new host
Right. Service accounts have a narrow, predictable pattern, so a different logon type and source stands out.
Expected activity, because service accounts may be used for admin tasks at any desk
Using a service account for hands-on admin work is poor practice and still a deviation from its normal pattern.

q.q: An executive account passes MFA from a new country and, minutes later, creates a mailbox rule forwarding mail to an outside address. What is the best next action?
o: Revoke active sessions, then verify with the executive by phone
Right. The forwarding rule suggests takeover, so contain access first and verify through a channel the attacker doesn't control.
Close the alert as travel, because the user passed MFA
MFA can be bypassed or approved by mistake, and the rule is a strong takeover sign.
Block the entire country for all users at the firewall
That disrupts everyone and doesn't remove the attacker's existing session.
Wait for a second alert before doing anything about the account
Waiting lets the attacker keep reading and forwarding mail.

q.q: A UEBA alert shows an HR analyst opened 15 more files than usual on the last day of the month. The files have no sensitive labels. What is the best next action?
o: Ignore it and don't record anything in the case system
An alert that is dropped without notes can't be reviewed later.
Verify with the supervisor and close with notes if justified
Right. A low-risk deviation with a plausible cause is resolved by quick verification and a documented decision.
Disable the account at once and start a legal hold on all of its data
This is far out of proportion to a small change with no sensitive data.
Escalate to the commanding officer as a major data breach right away
No evidence supports a breach, and unnecessary escalation wastes leadership attention.

q.q: NetFlow shows a 4 GB transfer from a file server to an outside address. The analyst wants to know if it contained Social Security numbers. Why can't NetFlow answer this?
o: NetFlow records are kept for only an hour by design
Retention is set by the collector's configuration. The content is the issue.
NetFlow records only the connections that the firewall blocked or dropped
Flow records cover allowed traffic as well, which is why they show the transfer.
NetFlow data is encrypted, so analysts can't read the records
The records themselves are readable. They just don't hold content.
Flow records show who talked to whom and how much, not the content
Right. Flow data holds addresses, ports and byte counts, not payloads.

q.q: An analyst captures a TLS 1.3 session with no decryption keys. Which detail is typically still visible?
o: IP addresses, ports, packet sizes and timing
Right. These sit outside the encrypted part, which is why encrypted traffic can still be profiled.
The cookies that the browser sent with each request
Cookies are HTTP headers, which are encrypted.
The response body that the server returned to the client
The body is encrypted along with the rest of the application data.
The full URL path and query string of each request
The path is inside the encrypted HTTP request.

q.q: In Wireshark, an analyst needs to save a file that was downloaded over plain HTTP in a capture. Which action does this?
o: Analyze > Expert Information
This lists protocol warnings and notes, not file content.
Follow > UDP Stream
HTTP downloads use TCP, so a UDP stream view isn't the right place.
File > Export Objects > HTTP
Right. This lists the files carried in HTTP responses and lets the analyst save them for analysis.
Statistics > Conversations
This summarizes traffic between pairs of hosts. It doesn't extract files.

q.q: A capture shows a 40-byte POST from 192.0.2.50 to 198.51.100.77 every 60 seconds, give or take 2 seconds, for six hours. Which is the best interpretation?
o: A user browsing the Internet
A person's browsing is irregular and loads many different sites.
A large file download in progress
A download has large packets flowing toward the client, not tiny POSTs on a timer.
A normal NTP time synchronization
NTP uses UDP port 123 and doesn't send HTTP POST requests.
Command-and-control beaconing
Right. Small requests at a steady interval to one outside host are the pattern of a check-in to a controller.

q.q: A detection rule looks for PowerShell with the text "-enc" in the command line. An attack using "-EncodedCommand" was missed. What is the best fix?
o: Alert on every PowerShell process launch
That would flood analysts with normal admin activity.
Match case-insensitively and cover the accepted forms of the parameter
Right. PowerShell accepts shortened and full names for the parameter, and capitalization varies.
Delete the rule and rely on the antivirus
Removing a rule gives up coverage, and antivirus may not catch this method.
Match only the exact text "-enc" but check the logs more often
Checking more often doesn't change what the rule matches.

q.q: A rule meant to flag administrator logons outside 08:00-18:00 local time fires at the wrong hours. The domain controllers log in UTC, while the rule uses local time. What is the best fix?
o: Shift the rule's hours by a fixed offset for every log source
One offset is wrong for sources that already log in local time, and it breaks when daylight saving time changes.
Convert timestamps to one time zone before comparing
Right. A mismatch in time zones shifts every event, so the rule must compare like with like.
Change the rule to compare hours on a 12-hour clock
The clock format doesn't change the offset between UTC and local time.
Widen the allowed hours until the alerts stop appearing
That hides the problem and also hides real after-hours activity.

q.q: An attacker used procdump to copy memory from lsass.exe on a workstation. Which ATT&CK technique is this?
o: T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
Right. Reading LSASS memory is how attackers pull logon secrets from a Windows host.
T1055 Process Injection
Injection runs code inside another process, which is a different action.
T1558.003 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
Kerberoasting requests service tickets from the domain, and it does not dump memory.
T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying
Spraying tries a few passwords across many accounts. It doesn't read memory.

q.q: Which statement is a PROCEDURE, rather than a tactic or a technique?
o: Persistence: the tactic of staying in the network after a reboot or logoff
This is a tactic, the goal of keeping access over time.
Phishing: the general technique of tricking people into opening or clicking
This is a technique, the general method used to reach a goal.
Initial Access: the tactic of getting a first foothold in the target network
This is a tactic: the attacker's goal at a stage of the attack.
A group sent a fake invoice whose macro ran an encoded PowerShell command
Right. A procedure is the specific way an actor carried out a technique.

q.q: Which TWO ATT&CK techniques belong to the persistence tactic? (Choose two.)
o: T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact
This is ransomware encryption, in the impact tactic.
T1547.001 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Right. A Run key entry starts a program each time a user logs on.
T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
Right. A scheduled task can start malware again after every reboot or at set times.
T1566.001 Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
This delivers the first foothold, in the initial access tactic.
T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
This steals credentials, which belongs to the credential access tactic.

q.q: A payment app keeps no record of who approved each transfer, so users can later claim they never approved one. Which STRIDE threat is this?
o: Repudiation
Right. Without an audit trail, a person can deny an action and nobody can prove otherwise.
Spoofing
Spoofing is pretending to be someone else. Here the real users made the transfers.
Tampering
Tampering is the unauthorized change of data. Nothing here says data was altered.
Information disclosure
Disclosure is exposure of data to people who shouldn't see it.

q.q: A team draws a data flow diagram of a new case system. Where should it focus controls first?
o: On internal processes that never touch another zone
Those carry less exposure than the points where outsiders connect.
At trust boundaries, where data crosses between zones
Right. Attacks and mistakes concentrate where data moves between less trusted and more trusted areas.
Inside the database engine only, away from the network
Protecting only the engine leaves the paths into it open.
On the external entities themselves, such as partner systems the team doesn't run
The team can't place controls on systems it doesn't own. It protects the boundary where their data enters.

q.q: A team has listed the system's assets and drawn how data flows between its parts. What is the next step in building the threat model?
o: Run a vulnerability scan on the live production network
A scan finds existing weaknesses but doesn't model design-level threats.
Write the final report for management and the owner
A report summarizes results. The threats haven't been found yet.
Identify threats at each flow, for example with STRIDE
Right. With assets and flows known, the team asks what could go wrong at each point.
Buy security tools for each asset on the list
Controls are chosen after threats are known and rated.

q.q: A user reports clicking a link in a phishing message and entering a password. Which TWO steps belong in the investigation and response? (Choose two.)
o: Reply to the sender and ask them to stop sending the message
Contacting the attacker gains nothing and confirms an active address.
Check sign-in logs for the account and reset its password and sessions
Right. Sign-ins show whether the stolen password was used, and the reset ends any access.
Wait a week to see whether any more users report the same message
Waiting leaves a stolen password usable.
Delete the user's mailbox and its backups to remove the evidence
Deleting the mailbox destroys evidence and disrupts the user.
Search mail and proxy logs for other recipients and who clicked
Right. This shows who else received the message and who clicked.

q.q: An employee who is leaving next week downloaded 8 GB from a shared case folder. What should the SOC do first?
o: Disable all of the employee's accounts without telling anyone
Acting alone without HR or legal can create legal problems and lose evidence of intent.
Confront the employee and ask them to delete the files
This warns the person and may destroy evidence.
Post a reminder about acceptable use for all staff
A general reminder does nothing about this activity.
Coordinate with HR and legal and quietly preserve the activity logs
Right. Insider cases involve policy and law, and preserving logs first protects the evidence.

q.q: After a password theft, which evidence best shows what the attacker actually did inside the victim's mailbox?
o: The mailbox audit log of items read and inbox rules created
Right. It records actions in the mailbox itself, such as reading mail or creating rules.
The VPN concentrator's bandwidth report for the user
It shows traffic volume, not mailbox actions.
The DHCP lease history for the user's laptop and phone
DHCP shows which addresses a device held, not mailbox actions.
The firewall's NAT translation table for the day
NAT entries map addresses and don't say what happened in an account.

q.q: A sample is packed. A hash lookup finds nothing, and the sandbox report shows no behavior because the file waited 20 minutes before doing anything. What should the analyst do next?
o: Mark the sample as benign because nothing happened in the sandbox
A quiet run in a time-limited sandbox doesn't show a file is safe.
Do more static analysis, such as unpacking, to find the delay
Right. Static work can reveal the wait and the hidden code that a short run missed.
Run the sample on a production workstation to see what it does
Running unknown malware on production risks real damage.
Delete the sample and close the case without a report
Closing the case ignores the sign that the file hides its behavior.

q.q: Where should an analyst detonate an unknown executable?
o: On a production server, inside a quarantine folder
A folder does not stop a process from running.
On the analyst's own work laptop with antivirus switched on
Antivirus is not a safe boundary, and the laptop holds work data and credentials.
In an isolated VM with simulated networking and a snapshot
Right. Isolation protects other systems, and snapshots let the analyst reset after each run.
In a virtual machine on the unit's normal staff VLAN
Malware could spread to neighbors or reach internal servers.

q.q: A sandbox run of a macro dropper is complete. Which package best lets other teams hunt for the same malware?
o: A note saying the sample is dangerous and should be avoided
A bare warning gives nothing to search for or detect.
The name one antivirus product gave the sample, with its version
Product names vary between vendors and can't be searched in logs.
The filename and a screenshot of the analyst's desktop session
Filenames change easily, and a screenshot adds nothing searchable.
Hashes, network indicators, behavior changes and ATT&CK mapping
Right. This gives both exact indicators and behaviors, so others can search logs and write detections.

q.q: A predictive model reports this sequence across two hosts: scanning of port 445 across a subnet, then a successful SMB logon to a file server, then growing outbound HTTPS traffic from that server. How should the analyst read it?
o: As a sign that the firewall has stopped working and needs repair
No evidence points to a firewall failure.
As lateral movement toward data theft, so contain the server
Right. The pattern fits an attack moving toward data theft, so containing the server first is sensible and the logs then confirm it.
As normal backup activity that the SOC can leave alone
Backups don't scan a subnet before logging in.
As a hardware fault in the file server's network card
A fault wouldn't scan other hosts or start outbound traffic.

q.q: A model reports an "87% likelihood of command-and-control beaconing" for a host with steady 30-second connections to an unknown address. What is the best way to use this?
o: Treat it as a lead and confirm with DNS, proxy and endpoint evidence
Right. A score ranks suspicion. Confirmation from independent data decides whether to act.
Treat it as proof and wipe the host immediately
A score isn't proof, and a wipe destroys the evidence.
Raise the alert threshold so that only scores above 95% appear
A higher bar hides real detections, and a steady beacon at 87% still deserves a look.
Ignore it because machine learning is unreliable
Models are useful leads, even though they need checking.

q.q: On a Windows workstation, which parent and child process pair is the strongest sign of a malicious document?
o: chrome.exe starting its own helper processes
Chrome uses many child processes for tabs and extensions.
explorer.exe starting chrome.exe
This is what happens when a user clicks a browser icon.
WINWORD.EXE starting powershell.exe
Right. Word has no normal reason to launch a command shell. This is a classic macro or exploit result.
services.exe starting svchost.exe
This is routine Windows startup behavior.

q.q: An IP camera is sending small packets to an unknown address and is also probing other devices on its VLAN. It can't run an agent. What is the best first action?
o: Factory reset the camera at once and set a new password
A reset destroys evidence and the default credentials may still let it be taken over again.
Leave it running and monitor it for a month
The device is attacking other hosts now.
Install antivirus on the camera over the network
Cameras and similar devices usually can't run antivirus.
Isolate it on the network and capture the traffic it sends
Right. This contains the device without changing it and gives the team evidence of what it is doing.

q.q: A managed phone shows a jailbreak warning and an unknown configuration profile. Which action fits the playbook?
o: Disable the user's account for all systems for the next month
A month-long lockout is out of proportion when the device alone can be restricted.
Allow it to keep working because the user needs mail for mission work
A compromised phone may expose mail and credentials.
Mark it non-compliant to block mail and apps, then collect logs
Right. Removing access limits the damage, and the logs help show what changed.
Ask the user to delete the profile and carry on as normal
The user can't be sure what the device now trusts, and the evidence would be lost.

q.q: Which of these is an indicator of ATTACK (IOA), not an indicator of compromise (IOC)?
o: Word spawning PowerShell that creates a scheduled task
Right. An IOA describes behavior that signals an attack in progress.
A malicious IP address that appears in a public threat feed
A listed address is an IOC.
A domain name that an attacker used in a campaign last year
A known domain is an IOC.
A SHA-256 hash of a file that is already known to be malicious
A hash is an IOC, evidence of a known item.

q.q: According to the Pyramid of Pain, which type of indicator is hardest for an attacker to change after being detected?
o: IP addresses
Attackers can switch hosting or proxies quickly.
File hashes
A single changed byte creates a new hash, so this is the easiest to change.
Domain names
New names are cheap to register, although it is a little more effort than changing an IP.
Tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs)
Right. Changing how an attacker works costs time and skill, so detecting behavior hurts the most.

q.q: A feed lists an IP address first reported 14 months ago. Which TWO actions reduce harm from stale indicators? (Choose two.)
o: Check whether it now belongs to a shared cloud or CDN range
Right. Old malicious addresses are often reassigned to harmless customers.
Block every address in the same country as the listed one
Country-wide blocks hit legitimate traffic and don't target the actual threat.
Add the address to the allowlist so it stops raising alerts
Allowing a reported address ignores the report instead of checking it.
Expire indicators after a set age unless they are reconfirmed
Right. Aging out keeps blocklists current and limits false blocks.
Keep every indicator forever so that the history stays complete
History belongs in the intelligence record, but enforcement lists need cleaning.

q.q: Each build of a malware family has a different hash. Across five sandbox runs of different builds, the same mutex name and the same Run key value name appear every time. What is the best use of this?
o: Collect the artifacts but never use them for detection
Unused indicators don't protect anyone.
Create a behavior-based indicator on that mutex and Run key value
Right. Artifacts that stay constant across builds catch variants that hash checks miss.
Block only the hash from the first run
A single hash will not match the other builds.
Ignore the artifacts because only hashes count as indicators
Behavior and artifacts are often longer-lived than hashes.

q.q: Which indicator is the best "complex" indicator for catching many variants of a macro dropper?
o: A file with the extension .docm that was saved in a user's Downloads folder
Many harmless documents use macros too.
An Office app launches a script that drops an executable and connects out
Right. Chaining several behaviors is hard to avoid and has fewer false alarms than one event alone.
A single registry key read by a system process
Reading a registry key is routine and not specific to malware.
Any process that opens an outbound network connection to the Internet on a standard port
This is common to nearly all software and would flood analysts.

q.q: A sample runs only if the machine has more than 4 GB of RAM, more than two CPUs and signs of mouse movement. In the sandbox it exits without doing anything. What does this mean?
o: The sample is harmless, because it did nothing when it was run
A quiet result from a file that tests its environment doesn't show it is harmless.
The sandbox is broken and should be replaced with a newer product
The behavior comes from the sample.
The sample is corrupt and can be safely deleted from the lab
A corrupt file wouldn't test for RAM, CPUs and mouse movement.
It is checking for a sandbox, so make the lab look more realistic
Right. Environment checks are a known evasion method.

q.q: A cloud audit log shows a new API key for a service account downloading 20,000 files from storage in one hour. What is the best next step?
o: Rotate the storage bucket's encryption key
Server-side encryption keys don't stop a credential that is allowed to read the objects through the service.
Block the downloader's IP address at the firewall
Cloud API calls can come from many addresses, and the key would still work from another one.
Revoke the key, keep the logs, and list the files read
Right. Revoking ends the loss, and the logs show the scope of exposure.
Delete the storage bucket to remove the data from the cloud
That destroys data and evidence and causes an outage.

q.q: A suspect copied case files from a laptop to a USB drive. Which source best shows that and which files were copied?
o: Endpoint DLP or EDR file-write telemetry
Right. The agent on the laptop sees device connections and file activity.
The DNS server query log for the laptop's address
DNS records name lookups and doesn't show file copies.
The VPN concentrator session logs for the user
These show remote sessions, not local device activity.
The perimeter firewall logs for the laptop's address
A USB copy never crosses the network edge.

q.q: An application's service account ran a very large SELECT on a table holding Social Security numbers at 02:00 from a host that does not normally query it. Which log shows exactly what data was queried?
o: The operating system boot log of the database server
A boot log records startup events and has no queries.
NetFlow from the database subnet
Flows show volume and endpoints but not the query.
The web server access log
It shows web requests, not the SQL statements run against the database.
The database audit log
Right. It records the account, source, statements and objects touched.

q.q: A vulnerable service is exposed to the Internet. The vendor has no patch yet. Which mitigation is best?
o: Run a vulnerability scan every day until a patch appears
More scans report the same flaw again but don't reduce the exposure.
Restrict access with firewall rules and add a WAF or IPS rule
Right. Reducing exposure and blocking the known attack pattern lowers risk until a patch is out.
Put the service behind a load balancer for more capacity
Capacity doesn't block exploitation of a flaw.
Rename the service and move it to an unusual port so scanners miss it
Hiding the name doesn't remove the flaw, and attackers scan by behavior as well.

q.q: A scan finds a known flaw in a library inside a container image running in production. What is the right remediation?
o: Rebuild the image with the updated library and redeploy the containers
Right. Containers are meant to be replaced from a fixed image, not patched in place.
Log in to each running container and update the library by hand
Manual changes are lost when the container is replaced or redeployed, and they make running containers differ from the image.
Limit the container's outbound network and keep the old image
This limits some damage, but the vulnerable library stays in place, so it is a stopgap and not a remediation.
Scan the running container again every hour
More scanning repeats the finding. The library is still vulnerable.

q.q: Which source shows that attackers have actually exploited a vulnerability in the wild?
o: A CVSS base score of 9.8
The base score rates severity if the flaw is exploited. It doesn't show that attackers are using it.
The flaw's listing in the National Vulnerability Database
The NVD lists and scores flaws whether or not anyone exploits them.
Its listing in CISA's KEV catalog
Right. KEV lists flaws with reliable evidence of active exploitation in the wild.
The date the CVE was first published
A publication date says nothing about attacker use.

q.q: Which CVSS v3.1 base vector describes the flaw that is easiest to exploit remotely?
o: AV:A/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N
The attacker must be on the adjacent network and hold a low-level account.
AV:P/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N
This requires physical access to the device.
AV:L/AC:H/PR:H/UI:R
This needs local access, a hard setup, high privileges and a user action.
AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N
Right. Network reachable, low complexity, no privileges and no user action need the least from an attacker.

q.q: Four findings are due for fixes this week, but only one can go first. Which should it be?
o: A medium-score flaw on an Internet-facing server that is listed in KEV
Right. Active exploitation on an exposed server outweighs a slightly lower score.
A low-score flaw on a public web server with customer data, reported yesterday
A low score and no KEV listing put this behind the first one.
A high-score flaw on an internal printer needing local access
The flaw needs local access to an internal device, and printers hold little data of value.
A critical-score flaw on a powered-off, isolated lab machine with no data
The score is high, but nothing can reach the machine and nothing is at stake.

q.q: An EDR console shows a scheduled task named "GoogleUpdateTask" on a finance laptop. It runs C:\Users\Public\up.exe every five minutes, while the real browser updater lives under Program Files. What should the analyst do first?
o: Reimage the laptop right away so the task is gone, then continue with other alerts
Reimaging at once destroys the file and the history that show what it did and who else is affected.
Leave it alone, since the task name matches a real vendor's updater and looks normal
A name is easy to copy. The path and the five-minute timing don't match the real updater.
Hash and copy the file, check its reputation, and search other hosts for the same task
Right. The path and timing don't fit the real updater, so save the file, check what it is, and see how widely it is installed.
Add the task name to the EDR allowlist so the alert stops repeating on that laptop
Allowlisting hides a likely persistence mechanism instead of looking into it.

q.q: An authorized test shows that a web form builds its database query by pasting the user's text into it, and the input ' OR '1'='1 returns every row. Which change removes the root cause?
o: Block the single quote character at the web application firewall only
A filter is a stopgap, and attackers have many ways to encode input around it.
Use parameterized queries so input is always treated as data
Right. The database receives the query and the values separately, so input can't change the query itself.
Run the web server under a different operating system account for each site
A separate account limits damage on the server, and it doesn't change how the query is built.
Hide the database error messages that the page shows to users
This hides clues for an attacker but the query is still built from raw input.

q.q: In CVSS v3.1, which metric group lets an organization adjust a score for its own systems, for example when the vulnerable host sits on an isolated network?
o: Temporal
Temporal metrics change with time and with the state of exploits and fixes, not with the local setting.
Environmental
Right. Environmental metrics reflect the organization's own setting and the importance of the affected asset.
Impact subscore
The impact subscore is just one input to the base score.
Base
Base metrics describe the flaw and don't change with where it is installed.

q.q: A cloud storage account may have leaked case files. Which TWO log sources show which objects were read and how access to them was granted? (Choose two.)
o: Storage access logs showing which objects were read, and by whom
Right. They show exactly which files were read, when, and with which identity.
Badge reader logs from the building entrance and parking gate
Badge logs record physical entry, which has no link to cloud storage reads.
Control-plane audit logs of permission and policy changes
Right. They show whether someone made the storage public or granted new access before the reads.
Endpoint antivirus logs from the SOC analysts' workstations
These show detections on analyst machines, not reads of cloud objects.
VPC flow logs to the storage endpoint and its subnet
Flow logs show connections and byte counts, but not which objects were read or by which identity.

q.q: An AI traffic model labels a host as "stage 1: reconnaissance" because it tried many ports on one server. Which later stage should the analyst watch for first?
o: Patch installation on the host that ran the probe
Patching is a defender activity and isn't a stage an attacker's scan leads to.
Large uploads to an outside address before any access has been gained
Data theft needs access first, so it normally comes later in the chain.
Exploitation or password guessing against the ports that answered
Right. Recon is followed by an attempt to use whatever the probe found open.
A ransom note on the probed server
Impact comes at the end of an attack, after access and movement.

q.q: A model flags this order of events on a server: a new service is installed, then a lookup of a rarely seen domain, then small outbound requests at regular intervals. What does the sequence most likely describe?
o: A user browsing the Internet after logging in to the server
Browsing is irregular and doesn't install services.
A backup job copying data to an offsite site
Backups send large amounts of data, not small repeated requests.
A normal software update followed by vendor telemetry
Updates come from known vendor domains and don't beat at fixed intervals to a rare domain.
Persistence followed by command-and-control check-ins
Right. A new service keeps the attacker on the host, and the regular requests fit beaconing.

q.q: A sequence model scores a slow attack low, even though each step was logged. The attacker waited several days between steps. What is the most likely reason?
o: The model's window is shorter than the gaps between steps
