Right. Sequence models link events inside a window, and long gaps break the link.
The model reads only DNS logs and ignores endpoint data
Sequence models normally combine several data sources.
Slow attacks produce more alerts than fast ones and swamp the model
A slow attack usually produces fewer alerts at any one time, which is why it hides.
Encrypted traffic can't be used by any detection model at all
Models can still use sizes, timing and metadata of encrypted traffic.

q.q: A predictive model says the likely next step after credential dumping on a workstation is lateral movement over SMB or RDP. Which preparation fits best?
o: Change the Wi-Fi passphrase for the whole building
Wi-Fi access isn't part of the predicted path.
Alert on new remote logons for those accounts and limit SMB and RDP
Right. This watches the predicted move and narrows the paths the attacker would use.
Block all outbound HTTPS traffic from every workstation in the whole unit
This disrupts normal work and doesn't address the predicted move inside the network.
Keep the web proxy logs for a longer time than the current policy requires
Retention helps later review, but it doesn't prepare for movement over SMB or RDP.

q.q: During static analysis of a suspicious executable, which output shows that it calls Windows functions used to inject code into other processes?
o: The file's size and compile timestamp
These help classify the file and are easy to forge, but they don't list the functions it uses.
The file's SHA-256 hash
A hash identifies the file but doesn't reveal what it can do.
The import table
Right. It lists the library functions the program calls, such as memory-writing and thread-creating ones.
The icon embedded in the file
Icons are cosmetic and often copied from real software.

q.q: A packet capture shows an executable downloaded over plain HTTP. What is the safest way to get the sample out for analysis?
o: Export the object from the capture and store it in a password-protected archive in the lab
Right. Exporting from the capture keeps the sample exactly as seen, and the archive stops accidental runs.
Download the file again from the live site with a normal browser
A fresh download may be a different file, and it touches the attacker's server from a work network.
Open the capture on the analyst's main workstation and double-click the file
Running the file on a work machine risks infection.
Copy the whole capture to a shared drive that all staff can reach
Placing live malware where many people can open it spreads the risk.

q.q: Sandbox results show that a sample decrypts a payload in memory, but the code is heavily obfuscated and the analyst needs to see how the decryption works. What is the next step?
o: Delete the sample to remove the risk
Deleting the sample ends the analysis without answering the question.
Run the same sandbox test again with a longer timeout only
A longer run repeats the outside view and wouldn't show how the code works.
Share the report with partners and stop, because the sandbox run is complete
Sharing is the last step, and the key question here is still unanswered.
Reverse engineer the sample with a disassembler or debugger
Right. Deeper code-level work reveals the routine that the sandbox could only show from outside.

q.q: A sandbox report lists several observations. Which one should NOT be used alone as a detection, because normal software does it too?
o: A DNS lookup of a well-known public time server
Right. Many harmless programs do this, so a rule on it would fire constantly.
A new service created from an executable in a temp folder
Services started from temp folders are uncommon in normal work.
A mutex name that appears in every run of the sample
A constant artifact like this is specific to the family.
A new Run key pointing to a program in the user's Public folder
Persistence from an unusual folder is a useful behavior to detect.

q.q: How can an indicator taken from a sandbox report be made more useful against later builds of the same malware?
o: Use the date and time at which the sandbox ran the sample
The analysis time says nothing about what the sample does.
Use the exact byte size of the executable file that the sample dropped
Size changes with each rebuild, so it matches only one build.
Use the sandbox's analysis ID as the value in the detection rule
The ID belongs to the sandbox's own record and never appears on a real host.
Describe the behavior, such as a document that starts a script
Right. Behavior stays the same when the attacker changes the file, so a rule on it matches new builds.

q.q: A sandbox report shows that a sample contacted 198.51.100.77. Before the analyst adds the address as a blocking indicator, what should be checked?
o: Whether the sandbox rated the whole file as malicious
The verdict is already known, and it doesn't say whether this address is safe to block.
Whether the address replies to a ping from the SOC
A reply only shows the host is up, and pinging it from a work network is unwise.
Whether it is shared infrastructure that many harmless sites also use
Right. A shared address could cause blocks of legitimate services, so the context matters before enforcement.
Whether the sample used the address on a weekday
The weekday has no bearing on whether blocking is safe.

q.q: Which statement about indicators of attack (IOAs) is true?
o: They are file hashes taken from earlier breaches and reused
Hashes from past breaches are indicators of compromise.
They focus on attacker behavior, so they can catch new malware
Right. Looking at what an actor is doing doesn't depend on having seen the file before.
They can be found only after data has been stolen from the unit
IOAs are used while an attack is under way, so they help before data is lost.
They are lists of IP addresses and domains from public threat feeds
Address lists are indicators of compromise.

q.q: How does EPSS differ from CVSS?
o: EPSS assigns the CVE identifier numbers to new flaws
CVE identifiers are assigned by CVE numbering authorities, not by EPSS.
EPSS is a list of flaws that the government has confirmed are being exploited
That describes the CISA KEV catalog.
EPSS estimates how likely a flaw is to be exploited soon, while CVSS rates its severity
Right. A severity score and an exploitation estimate answer different questions, and triage uses both.
EPSS rates the damage a flaw could do, while CVSS predicts exploitation
This reverses the two scores.

q.q: Which example is orchestration, as opposed to simple automation?
o: A script that closes alerts when they are exact duplicates of an open case
This is a single automated task in one tool.
An analyst copying an address from the SIEM into a search box
This is manual work, with no tool coordination.
A scheduled report emailed to the SOC manager every Monday morning
This is a single scheduled task and not a coordinated multi-tool flow.
One workflow that enriches an IP, opens a ticket and blocks it
Right. Orchestration coordinates tasks across several tools in one process.

q.q: Which job is a SOAR platform designed to do better than a SIEM?
o: Run repeatable response steps across several tools
Right. SOAR connects to the security stack and carries out playbooks.
Collect and store logs from every device in the company
Log collection and storage is the core job of a SIEM or data platform.
Block packets at the network edge at line speed
Packet filtering is done by a firewall or IPS.
Scan servers for missing patches each week
That is the job of a vulnerability scanner.

q.q: In Cisco XDR automation workflows, what is a target?
o: The analyst who approves the workflow's actions
People approve or run steps, but they are not targets.
A system or resource that the workflow communicates with
Right. Workflows use activities that connect to targets such as other security products.
A suspicious file that the workflow is analyzing
A file would be an observable or an input, not a target.
The incident that the workflow was created to close
The incident is the case being worked, not a system the workflow connects to.

q.q: What does this Python script print?
o: Nothing, because raise_for_status() always stops the script
raise_for_status() raises an error only when the response is a failure (4xx or 5xx).
The values of indicators whose score is 80 or higher
Right. The loop keeps only items that meet the score test and prints their value.
The scores of indicators below 80
The condition checks for 80 or more and prints the value, not the score.
Every indicator value in the response, whatever its score
The if statement filters items, so not every value is printed.

q.q: The log lines look like: "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 51234 ssh2". What does this script output?
o: A list of addresses with more than five failed logins
Right. split()[-4] picks the address, and the dictionary counts lines per address.
The total number of failures across the whole log file
The script outputs addresses, not a total.
The list of usernames that were guessed in the attempts
The code reads the address field, not the user name.
The five most recent failed attempts from the log file
The script has no recency logic and no limit of five items.

q.q: Why does this script build a set instead of a list?
o: A set lets the script write to the CSV file
Writing to a file needs a file object. The set type has no role.
A set encrypts the hashes in memory
Python sets don't encrypt anything.
A set gives fast membership checks and removes duplicates
Right. Looking up a hash in a set is quick, even with a very large IOC file.
A set keeps the hashes in the order they were read
Sets don't promise any order. A list would keep order.

q.q: A script prints every IP found in logs. The analyst wants it to skip private addresses. Which line, placed before the print, does this?
o: if len(ip) < 7 or len(ip) > 15: break
Length doesn't show whether an address is private, and break would stop the whole loop.
if ip.isdigit() or ip.isalpha(): continue
An address has digits and dots together, so neither test is true and nothing would be skipped.
if ip.startswith("10.") or ip.startswith("172."): continue
This misses 192.168.0.0/16, and 172. also matches public addresses outside 172.16.0.0/12.
if ipaddress.ip_address(ip).is_private: continue
Right. The standard library knows every private range, and continue skips to the next address.

q.q: A script that looks up 2,000 hashes in a reputation API begins to receive HTTP 429 responses. Which change fits best?
o: Switch every call to HEAD requests to save bandwidth
The API may not support HEAD, and the limit counts requests of every kind.
Retry immediately in a tight loop until a call works
This sends even more requests and makes the limit worse.
Honor Retry-After, sleep that long, and retry a few times
Right. This respects the server's limit and avoids an endless loop.
Remove the timeout so that each call waits longer for an answer
A timeout limit isn't what caused the 429s, and removing it can make the script hang.

q.q: A script has the API key written inside it. Which change best improves security?
o: Move the key into a comment in the script
Comments are as readable as code, and still in the file.
Encode the key with Base64 inside the script file
Base64 is an encoding that anyone can reverse. It isn't protection.
Put the key in a config file that is committed with the script
The key would still sit in the repository and its history.
Read the key from an environment variable or secrets manager
Right. The key then stays out of the script file and out of the code repository.

q.q: A response body is: {"data": {"verdict": {"score": 90, "tags": ["c2", "dropper"]}}}. In Python, which expression returns "c2"?
o: r.json()["data"]["verdict"]["tags"][1]
Index 1 is the second item, "dropper".
r.json()["data"]["verdict"]["tags"][0]
Right. It follows the keys data, verdict and tags, then takes the first list item.
r.json()["data"]["tags"][0]
The tags list is inside verdict, so this path raises a KeyError.
r.json()["verdict"]["tags"][0]
There is no top-level verdict key.

q.q: An alert export has a different number of related IP addresses per alert. Which format keeps this structure most cleanly for a script?
o: JSON, with the addresses in an array under each alert
Right. JSON supports nested lists of varying length.
An HTML table for display
HTML is designed for showing content to people, not for scripts to read data.
CSV with one row per alert and addresses packed into one column
CSV is flat, so a list in a cell needs a custom separator and breaks when a value contains it.
A plain syslog line per alert
Free text needs custom parsing for every field.

q.q: Which task is the best candidate for full automation in a SOAR platform?
o: Looking up the reputation of every URL and hash in each new alert
Right. It is repetitive, rule-based and low risk, so no judgment is needed.
Approving a change to the unit's firewall design
Design changes need review and accountability.
Deciding whether to terminate an employee who violated policy
That is a human decision with legal and personnel effects.
Telling the commanding officer about a serious breach
Leadership notifications need human judgment about wording and timing.

q.q: A SOAR platform uses a machine learning model to auto-close alerts it scores as benign. What safeguard is most important?
o: Hide the auto-closed alerts so analysts aren't distracted
Hiding them removes the chance to spot errors.
Set the confidence level to 100% so it closes only perfect matches
A model rarely reaches 100%, so this would turn the feature off.
Let the model retrain itself with no oversight
Unchecked retraining can learn from its own mistakes.
Sample the auto-closed alerts for human review and track the missed-threat rate
Right. Reviews show whether the model hides real attacks and let the team retrain it.

q.q: A script must check 5,000 hashes against an API that allows 100 requests per minute. The API also offers a bulk endpoint that accepts 100 hashes per call. What is the best approach?
o: Split the work between several API keys to dodge the limit
Sharing keys to avoid rate limits usually breaks the provider's terms.
Send 5,000 single requests at once from several threads
This breaks the limit quickly and may get the key blocked.
Use the bulk endpoint and pace the calls to stay within the limit
Right. Batching reduces requests to 50, and pacing avoids hitting 429 responses.
Check only the first 100 hashes and skip the rest
Skipping data gives incomplete results.

q.q: A script that calls an internal API sometimes freezes forever when the server doesn't answer. What is the correct fix?
o: Increase the number of hashes per request
Larger payloads can make timeouts more likely.
Set an explicit request timeout and handle the timeout error
Right. A limit on waiting time lets the script fail cleanly or retry.
Remove error handling so the script stops at the first problem
Without handling, one slow call can still hang or crash the whole run.
Send each request twice in case one gets lost
Duplicates add load and do nothing about waiting forever.

q.q: A script that pulls all alerts from an API always reports exactly 100 alerts, though the portal shows 3,200. Which TWO changes fix this and catch it if it happens again? (Choose two.)
o: Rotate the API key every time a request is sent to the API
The key doesn't control the page size.
Follow the API's pagination until no next page remains
Right. The API returns results in pages, so the script must keep asking for the next one.
Add a longer timeout to the first request to the API
The data arrives. It is just cut at one page.
Compare the total count with the records collected and alert on a gap
Right. A count check shows right away when data is missing, instead of letting a silent gap go unnoticed.
Convert the response from JSON to CSV before parsing it
The format doesn't change how many records the API returns per call.

q.q: A script calls a REST API with an expired token and the response is 401 Unauthorized. Which action fits?
o: Change the HTTP method from GET to POST
The method isn't the cause of the failure.
Request a new token and retry once
Right. 401 means the credentials are missing or not valid, so a fresh token is the fix.
Wait and retry later, because the server is overloaded
Overload produces 503 responses, not 401.
Retry the same request every second until it works
The same bad token will fail every time.

q.q: A script gets HTTP 429 with the header Retry-After: 30. What does it mean?
o: The server crashed and will reboot in 30 seconds
A server failure produces a 5xx code.
The server could not find the resource and will create it in 30 seconds
A missing resource gives 404, and nothing is created.
The user is signed in but has no permission to use this endpoint
That is 403 Forbidden.
The client sent too many requests and should wait about 30 seconds
Right. 429 is the standard status for rate limiting, and Retry-After says how long to wait.

q.q: A gateway in front of a security API returns 504 Gateway Timeout for a request that worked an hour ago. What is the most likely meaning?
o: The URL path in the request is wrong and should be corrected
A wrong path returns 404, and the same request worked an hour ago.
The client's token expired and must be renewed before the next call
That would return 401.
The upstream server was too slow, so retry later with a backoff
Right. 5xx codes point at the server side, and 504 means the upstream didn't reply in time.
The request body failed validation and needs a corrected field
A bad body gives a 4xx code, such as 400 or 422.

q.q: A script receives the response shown. Where does it find how many requests it has left in the current window?
o: In the X-RateLimit-Remaining header
Right. Headers carry metadata such as rate limit counts, which the script can read before sending more.
In the request's URL query string
The URL belongs to the request. This is the response.
In the status line, next to the 200 code
The status line holds the version, code and reason phrase, here 200 OK.
In the JSON body, next to the verdict
The body has the verdict. The limit information is in headers here.

q.q: A script calls response.json() and fails with a parse error, though the status is 200. The response has Content-Type: text/html. What is the most likely cause?
o: The script used the wrong HTTP method for this call to the API
A wrong method usually returns 405 or another error status.
The server sent a 200 in error, so the data in the body was lost
A 200 status doesn't mean the body is the expected format.
The API only supports XML responses, not JSON
The header says HTML, not XML.
The body is an HTML page, such as a login or block page
Right. The content type says HTML, so a JSON parser fails.

q.q: An eavesdropper captures this header from a request sent over plain HTTP: Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46U3VwZXJTZWNyZXQ=. What can they do?
o: Read the password only if they also know the server's private key
No key is involved, because the value is merely encoded.
Decode the Base64 and read the user name and password
Right. Basic authentication only encodes the credentials, and anyone can decode them.
Reuse it only for one request, because it is a one-time token
It's the same password for every request until it is changed.
Nothing, because the value is encrypted
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.

q.q: A script sends its API key as https://tip.example.org/api?api_key=KEY123. What is the main risk of this?
o: URLs are often logged by proxies and servers, so the key leaks
Right. Keys in URLs end up in many logs. A header is a safer place.
The server will reject every request with a 500 error
Servers accept this form when the API supports it.
HTTPS cannot be used with a query string at all, so it is sent in clear
HTTPS works with query strings, and the string is protected in transit. The problem is where it gets stored.
The key becomes shorter once it is placed in a URL and can't be used
Where the key is placed doesn't change its length.

q.q: A script that logs in to an API gets a token valid for one hour. Every day, about an hour after it starts, the script begins getting 401 errors. What is the best fix?
o: Restart the server every hour on the hour
Restarting a server has no effect on a client's expired token.
Send the password with every request instead of a token
Sending the password each time exposes it more often.
Request a new token when the old one expires
Right. Tokens are short-lived by design, so the script must renew them.
Ask the vendor for a token that never expires
Tokens without expiry raise risk if leaked.

q.q: An analyst sets TIP_KEY=abc123 in a shell and then runs a Python script that reads os.environ["TIP_KEY"]. The script reports the variable missing. What is the likely reason?
o: The variable was set without export, so child processes don't inherit it
Right. A plain assignment is local to the shell. Export makes it available to programs the shell starts.
Python can't read environment variables in a script
Python reads them through os.environ.
Environment variables work only in uppercase and the name had a digit
Names can contain digits and uppercase letters.
The shell deleted the variable when the command ended
The shell keeps its variables until it exits.

q.q: Which command lists log files under /var/log whose names end in .log and that changed in the last 24 hours?
o: cd /var/log && pwd
This changes directory and prints the path, with no search.
find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +1
+1 selects files modified more than one day ago.
ls -S /var/log/*.log
This sorts files by size and doesn't filter by time.
find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1
Right. -mtime -1 selects files modified less than one day ago.

q.q: What does this pipeline show?
q.code: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5
o: The first five lines of access.log, in sorted order
head works after the counting and shows the top counted values, not the first lines.
The last five lines that were written to access.log by the web server
tail would do that, and this pipeline counts unique values.
The five most common first-column values, with counts
Right. It extracts the first field, counts duplicates, sorts by count, and shows the top five.
The five largest files in the current working folder on disk
Nothing in it measures file sizes.

q.q: In a CI/CD pipeline, which component stores the built, versioned output that is later deployed?
o: The target environment where the release runs
The environment runs the release. It isn't where versioned builds are kept.
The artifact repository
Right. It holds build results, such as packages and images, so the same tested build moves to each environment.
The build runner that executes the pipeline jobs
The runner executes the jobs. It isn't the versioned store for their results.
The source code repository
That stores source code and history, not built outputs.

q.q: A pipeline deploys to production automatically whenever unit tests pass. Security wants to stop releases that carry serious findings. Which change fits best?
o: Move all security scans to run after the production release
Late scanning finds problems after users are exposed.
Add a gate that fails builds with critical findings
Right. A gate in the pipeline stops builds with serious findings before they reach production.
Remove the unit tests so the pipeline finishes sooner
Tests improve quality and don't slow security scans.
Email a security report to the developers once each quarter
Quarterly reports can't stop a release.

q.q: Which practice best reflects "shift left" in DevOps?
o: Fix vulnerabilities only after customers report them
That is the opposite of shifting left.
Write the security policy after the product ships
Policy written afterward can't guide design and build choices.
Run one large penetration test a month before launch
This is late in the process.
Run code and dependency scans on every pull request
Right. Finding problems early, when the code is written, is cheaper and safer.

q.q: A team ships one big release every quarter with manual checklists, and most bugs and vulnerabilities are found at the end. Which change fits DevOps principles?
o: Ship larger releases less often so reviews can be longer
Bigger batches increase risk and delay feedback.
Skip testing in the final week to save time
Skipping tests increases risk.
Ship small changes often, with automated tests and fast feedback
Right. Small automated releases find problems sooner and are easier to roll back.
Have developers and operations teams work in separate groups
DevOps aims to bring the groups together.

q.q: A server was built from infrastructure as code, but an admin changed a firewall rule by hand in the console. The next pipeline run quietly reverts it. What is this problem called, and what is the proper fix?
o: Configuration drift; make the change in code, then redeploy
Right. Manual changes differ from the declared state. Editing the code keeps everything repeatable and reviewed.
Privilege escalation; remove the admin's account from the console
The admin was allowed to log in and make the change. The issue is the process.
Version skew; lock the console so that nobody can ever log in
The term doesn't fit, and locking everyone out isn't practical.
Data remanence; wipe the server and rebuild it from scratch
Remanence is about leftover data, not configuration differences.

q.q: A Terraform file defines a security group that allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Which control catches this before deployment?
o: DAST against the deployed environment
DAST tests a running application after deployment, and it doesn't read a Terraform file before it is applied.
Cloud configuration drift detection after deployment
Drift detection finds changes after the fact. It doesn't stop the file before deployment.
A password change for the cloud account
Passwords are unrelated to what the file allows.
A policy-as-code scan of the IaC files in the pipeline
Right. Scanning the code finds risky settings before they reach the cloud.

q.q: What does it mean that IaC tools are "declarative"?
o: You describe the desired end state and the tool works out the changes needed
Right. The tool compares the declared state with the real one and makes changes to match.
The tool decides which security settings to use without your input
The settings are in the code you write.
You write each command in the exact order the server must run it
That is imperative scripting.
You must edit servers by hand and record the steps afterward
That is manual administration, not code.

q.q: Which TWO practices keep an API key safe in a script? (Choose two.)
o: Put it in the URL query string so it is easy to test
URLs are logged in many places, so the key would leak.
Send it in a request header over HTTPS
Right. A header over an encrypted connection is not logged like a URL and can't be read in transit.
Share one key among every script on the team so rotation is easy
A shared key can't be traced to one script, and one leak exposes every script.
Read it from a secrets manager or an environment variable
Right. The key stays out of the script and the repository, and it can be rotated in one place.
Commit it to a private branch so teammates can find it
Anyone with repository access can read it, and it stays in the history.

q.title: Map one attack chain from the SIEM export to MITRE ATT&CK
q.scenario: The SOC got an alert for workstation WS221. You are authorized to review this export from the SIEM, which joins mail gateway, EDR, proxy and Windows logs for the same morning. Mark every line that is part of the attack. Then pick the order of ATT&CK tactics the attacker followed.
q.ticket: INC-8812: EDR alert on WS221 (user jsmith). WS221 is 192.0.2.21. svc_backup also runs the backup agent on WS221. Scope: review of the exported logs only. Addresses and domains are examples.

lines.text: 08:00:03 WinSec 4624 Logon type=5 (service) user=svc_backup host=FS02 src=-
lines.why: The backup service logs on at 08:00 every day. A service logon at a set time is routine.

lines.text: 08:55:12 MailGW delivered from=billing@invoice-pay.example to=jsmith@unit.example attach=Invoice_4471.docm
lines.why: A lookalike sender with a macro-enabled attachment. This is initial access by phishing, T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment.

lines.text: 09:02:40 EDR proc_create host=WS221 parent=WINWORD.EXE child=powershell.exe cmd="powershell -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA..."
lines.why: Word starting a hidden PowerShell with an encoded command is execution, T1059.001. Office programs have no normal reason to do this.

lines.text: 09:02:41 EDR proc_create host=WS221 parent=explorer.exe child=chrome.exe user=jsmith
lines.why: A user opened the browser from the desktop. The parent is explorer.exe, which is normal.

lines.text: 09:03:05 Proxy GET http://cdn-files.example/up/upd.exe 200 bytes_in=412000 user=jsmith
lines.why: The PowerShell command downloaded an executable from an unfamiliar site. This is ingress tool transfer, T1105.

lines.text: 09:03:30 EDR reg_set host=WS221 key=HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run value=Updater data=C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Roaming\upd.exe
lines.why: A Run key entry starts the dropped file at every logon. This is persistence, T1547.001.

lines.text: 09:10:12 EDR proc_access host=WS221 source=upd.exe target=lsass.exe access=VM_READ
lines.why: A user-folder program reading the memory of lsass.exe is credential dumping, T1003.001.

lines.text: 09:12:30 Proxy CONNECT status-check.example:443 bytes_out=210 bytes_in=190 (repeats every 60 s)
lines.why: Small, regular connections to one rarely seen site are command-and-control beaconing, T1071.001.

lines.text: 09:15:30 DNS query intranet.example.org A -> 10.1.1.5 client=WS221
lines.why: WS221 resolved an internal site name to an internal address. This is ordinary use.

lines.text: 09:20:15 Proxy GET https://update.vendor.example/patch 200 user=jsmith
lines.why: A request to the software vendor's own update site is a normal, expected download.

lines.text: 09:30:44 WinSec 4624 Logon type=10 (RDP) user=svc_backup host=FS02 src=192.0.2.21
lines.why: The backup account logs on by remote desktop from WS221 (192.0.2.21), though it only ever runs as a service. Valid account use for lateral movement: T1021.001 with T1078.

lines.text: 09:41:20 EDR proc_create host=FS02 child=7z.exe cmd="7z a C:\Temp\x.7z D:\Case_Files\* -p..."
lines.why: Files were packed into a password-protected archive in a temp folder. This is collection, T1560.001.

lines.text: 09:52:08 Proxy POST https://files-share.example/upload bytes_out=388000000 user=svc_backup
lines.why: A 388 MB upload from the backup account to a file-sharing site. This is exfiltration over a web service, T1567.

lines.text: 10:15:00 Backup job completed host=FS02 status=success
lines.why: The routine job finished with a normal status. It has no link to the attack.

ask.label: Leaving out the command-and-control traffic (T1105, T1071.001), which ran alongside the other steps, in what order did the attacker move through the remaining ATT&CK tactics?
opts: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Credential Access, Lateral Movement, Collection, Exfiltration
Initial Access, Execution, Credential Access, Persistence, Collection, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration
Reconnaissance, Execution, Credential Access, Persistence, Exfiltration, Lateral Movement, Collection
Execution, Initial Access, Persistence, Lateral Movement, Credential Access, Collection, Exfiltration
ask.why: The timestamps give the order: the phishing mail came first, then PowerShell, the Run key, the LSASS read, the RDP logon, the archive and the upload. In the other options persistence and credential access are swapped, or lateral movement and collection are out of place, or Execution comes before Initial Access. Command and control (the agent download and the 60-second beacon) runs underneath the whole chain, so it isn't placed in this list.

q.title: Check a file hash against the threat intelligence API
q.scenario: A phishing attachment was handed to the SOC. You are authorized to look up its MD5 hash in the unit's internal threat intelligence platform (TIP) from this lab host. Use only read requests. The API wants a bearer token, which is already in the TIP_TOKEN variable. The base URL is in TIP_BASE and the hash is in HASH. Find the verdict, find related indicators, and keep the token and the service safe.
q.ticket: INC-8830: look up hash 9e107d9d372bb6826bd81d3542a419d6 in the TIP. Read-only (GET). Do not print the token. Do not scan or contact the related addresses.
q.intro: soc-lab (analyst, curl and jq installed). Type a command, or help.

cmds.out:
TIP lab notes
Base URL is in $TIP_BASE and the hash to check is in $HASH.
The token is in $TIP_TOKEN. Send it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.
Read-only task: GET requests only. Limit: 60 requests per minute.

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"missing or invalid token"}
Not run: printing the token puts a secret on the screen and in the history. Use it inside the header without printing it.
Not run: -k turns off certificate checking, so an on-path attacker could read the token. Fix the trust problem instead.
Not run: this task is read-only. Changing or adding indicators needs a separate approval.
Not run: the ticket allows lookups in the TIP only. Contacting the related addresses is out of scope and can alert the attacker.

checks.t: Sent an authenticated GET and got the verdict
checks.why: A GET with the Authorization: Bearer header returns 200 OK with a JSON body. The verdict is malicious with a score of 92. Without the header, the same request returns 401.

checks.t: Pulled single fields out of the JSON with jq
checks.why: jq turns a long body into just the field you need, such as the verdict or the related values, which is easier to put in a ticket.

checks.t: Listed the indicators related to the hash
checks.why: The related endpoint returns a domain and an IP address. These are candidates to search for in DNS and proxy logs.

checks.t: Did not print the token or turn off certificate checking
checks.why: A printed token can end up in history, tickets or screenshots, and -k removes the check that you are talking to the real server. Use the token only in the header over verified HTTPS.

checks.t: Made no changes to the TIP and did not contact the related addresses
checks.why: The ticket allows read-only lookups. Writing to the TIP or touching the related addresses is outside your approval and may tip off the attacker.

q.title: Order the response to a reported phishing email
q.scenario: A user reported a message with a link to a fake sign-in page. The SOC's SOAR platform will run this play. Add the steps that belong, in the order they should happen. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: INC-8841: user-reported phishing. The incident plan authorizes the SOC to quarantine mail and block domains. Several people may have received the message.

rules.text: Save the original message with its full headers to the case
rules.why: The original message and headers are the evidence. Save them before anything changes the mail system.

rules.text: Pull the URL and any file hashes and check their reputation
rules.why: The indicators are needed to know what to search for and what to block.

rules.text: Search mail and proxy logs for other recipients and for users who visited the link
rules.why: This shows how far the message spread and who might have entered a password.

rules.text: Quarantine the message from every mailbox and block the domain and URL
rules.why: This stops further exposure. It needs the saved evidence and the indicators from the earlier steps.

rules.text: Reset the passwords and revoke the sessions of users who entered credentials
rules.why: Only users who really submitted a password need this, and the scope search tells you who they are.

rules.text: Record the findings in the ticket and tune the mail filter rules
rules.why: Documenting the case closes the loop, and rule changes help catch similar mail next time.

rules.text: Reset the passwords of every recipient before checking who clicked
rules.why: This is over-broad and disruptive. Scope the exposure first, then reset only the accounts that need it.

rules.text: Open the link from an analyst workstation's normal browser to confirm it is phishing
rules.why: Opening a suspected phishing link on a normal workstation risks infection and a leaked sign-in. Use the sandbox or URL detonation.

rules.text: Reply to the sender to say the message was reported
rules.why: A reply confirms a live mailbox to the attacker and may bring more targeted mail.

before.why: Save the evidence before you quarantine or block anything, since those actions change the mail system.
You need the URL and hashes to know what to block.
Find out who clicked and who entered credentials before choosing whose accounts to reset.

last.why: The write-up and tuning come last, when the facts are complete.

q.title: Place the parts of a SOC data and response flow
q.scenario: A unit's SOC is setting up how data and actions flow from log sources to response. Place each part in the right spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong in this design.
q.ticket: Design review SOC-5. Rules: logs are collected in one place, outside intelligence is checked before it is acted on, and every automated response leaves a record.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: first stop for data leaving the log sources

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: receives from Stage 1 and raises alerts from patterns across sources

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: feeds vetted context to Stage 2 and decides what is trusted

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: receives alerts from Stage 2 and acts on them in several other tools

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: receives instructions from Stage 4 and changes the state of a system

slots.label: Spot F
slots.hint: keeps a record of what Stage 4 did and who approved it

devs.name: Log collector or forwarder
devs.why: A collector gathers logs from many sources in one place, so the analytics see a complete picture.

devs.name: SIEM
devs.why: The SIEM normalizes the data and correlates events across sources to raise alerts.

devs.name: Threat intelligence platform
devs.why: A TIP aggregates feeds, scores and expires indicators, and shares only vetted ones with the SIEM and other tools.

devs.name: SOAR platform
devs.why: SOAR receives alerts and runs playbooks across the other tools, pausing for approval where needed.

devs.name: Firewall and EDR
devs.why: These carry out the blocking and host isolation. SOAR sends the commands through their APIs.

devs.name: Case management system
devs.why: A case record keeps the ticket, evidence and approvals, so each automated step can be reviewed later.

devs.name: Public IOC feed to firewall
devs.why: Unvetted indicators sent directly to enforcement skip scoring and review, and can block legitimate services.

devs.name: Network TAP / packet broker
devs.why: A TAP copies packets for sensors. It doesn't forward event logs, so it doesn't fill the log-collection spot.

devs.name: Vulnerability scanner
devs.why: A scanner finds weaknesses on a schedule. It doesn't collect events, raise alerts or run responses.

devs.name: IDS sensor in passive mode
devs.why: It can alert but can't block, so it can't carry out the enforcement step.

q.title: Decide what a user behavior alert means
q.scenario: The SIEM's user behavior analytics raised a high-risk score for mlopez, an HR analyst. You are authorized to review the account's activity export. Mark every line that is part of the suspicious activity, then choose the best next action.
q.ticket: Alert UEBA-2290: risk score 94 for mlopez. Normal pattern: VPN from the home ISP, office hours, about 20 MB of file reads a day.

lines.text: Mon 08:02 VPN login user=mlopez src=203.0.113.50 (home ISP, usual) MFA=approved 1 prompt
lines.why: This is the normal pattern: the usual home address and a single MFA approval.

lines.text: Mon 08:10 CaseApp open user=mlopez; read 12 files (18 MB) from HR share
lines.why: The volume matches the user's usual daily reads.

lines.text: Mon 14:10 Print job user=mlopez pages=3 printer=HR-PRN1
lines.why: A small print job from the work printer is routine.

lines.text: Tue 02:14 VPN login user=mlopez src=192.0.2.88 (hosting provider, new country)
lines.why: The login comes from a new country, from a hosting provider rather than a home connection, and at 02:14. All three differ from the baseline.

lines.text: Tue 02:16 MFA push user=mlopez prompts=9 in 3 minutes, last approved
lines.why: Nine prompts in three minutes, then an approval, fits MFA fatigue. Someone else may be triggering the prompts.

lines.text: Tue 02:21 Mailbox rule created user=mlopez: forward mail containing "payroll" to an outside address
lines.why: A forwarding rule to an outside address is a common step after account takeover, so the attacker can read mail later.

lines.text: Tue 02:25 FileServer read user=mlopez bytes=4100000000 from HR share
lines.why: 4.1 GB in minutes, against a usual 20 MB a day. This is a large, fast collection of data.

lines.text: Tue 02:40 Proxy POST user=mlopez to personal-cloud.example bytes_out=3900000000
lines.why: Nearly all of that data was then uploaded to a personal cloud storage site. This is likely exfiltration.

lines.text: Tue 09:00 Badge in user=mlopez building=Admin door=Main
lines.why: A normal morning arrival. It doesn't show whether the account was used by someone else overnight, but the badge itself is not part of the suspicious activity.

ask.label: What is the best next action?
opts: Revoke the user's sessions and tokens, preserve the logs, and call the user on a known number
Close the alert as a false positive, because the user approved the MFA prompt and badged in at 09:00
Lower the risk score and wait for tomorrow's activity to update the user's baseline
Block personal-cloud.example at the proxy and leave the account and its sessions as they are
ask.why: The mix of a new location, repeated MFA prompts, a forwarding rule and a large copy and upload points to account takeover. Contain access first, keep the evidence, and verify with the user through a channel the attacker doesn't control. An approved MFA prompt can be forced by fatigue. Waiting or blocking one site leaves the attacker in the account.

q.title: Pick behavior-based indicators from a sandbox report
q.scenario: You ran a macro document in the unit's approved, isolated sandbox. Five runs of different builds gave the same behavior, but the file hash changed each time. Mark every line that would make a good behavior-based indicator for a detection rule. Leave the lines that normal software also does, or that change from run to run.
q.ticket: Analysis A-4410: approved sandbox, no production access. Goal: indicators that catch other builds of this sample.

lines.text: Process tree: WINWORD.EXE -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
lines.why: An Office program starting a hidden, encoded PowerShell is rare in normal work and stays the same across builds.

lines.text: File created: C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\a8f3.exe, written by powershell.exe
lines.why: A script engine dropping an executable into a temp folder is a strong behavior. The file name may change, but the pattern of dropping and running does not.

lines.text: Registry set: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run value=Updater data=...\a8f3.exe
lines.why: A new Run entry for a program in a user folder is a persistence behavior that held in all five runs.

lines.text: Mutex created: Global\Mx-7731-Q (seen in all 5 runs)
lines.why: A fixed mutex name that appears in every build is a stable artifact that catches variants a hash would miss.

lines.text: Network: HTTPS to one outside address every 60 seconds, about 200 bytes each time
lines.why: A regular small check-in is a beaconing pattern. The timing and size pattern outlasts a change of file hash.

lines.text: Network: DNS query for time.windows.com
lines.why: Windows looks up its time server as part of normal operation, so this would fire on every machine.

lines.text: Module loaded: C:\Windows\System32\kernel32.dll
lines.why: Nearly every program loads this system library, so it says nothing about this sample.

lines.text: Process: svchost.exe started by services.exe
lines.why: This is routine Windows startup behavior.

lines.text: SHA-256 of the dropped file: 2c26b46b68ffc68ff99b453c1d30413413422d706483bfa0f98a5e886266e7ae (different in every run)
lines.why: A hash that changes with each build only matches that one build, so it isn't a behavior-based indicator.

lines.text: Sandbox analysis ID: 88231-A
lines.why: This label belongs to the sandbox's own record and is not something the sample does.

ask.label: Why are the marked lines better indicators than the file hash?
opts: They describe behavior that stays the same when the attacker rebuilds the file and changes its hash
They can be blocked at the firewall, unlike a hash
They have no false positives on normal hosts
They are atomic indicators that have the same lifespan as the hash
ask.why: Rebuilding changes a hash with one byte but doesn't change what the program has to do to work. Behavior and fixed artifacts therefore catch variants. Firewalls can't block a process tree or a registry key. These rules can still fire on some normal software and need tuning. A hash is an atomic indicator that lasts only one build.
